content.thinking:
I'm thinking through the League of Legends art style requirements—bold saturated shapes, glowing magic accents, readability from a top-down view—and sketching out the scythe's realistic proportions, roughly 1.9m shaft with a 0.9m blade, plus how it should rest on a display stand touching the ground.

I'll go with an upright pose at a slight 8° lean, anchored into a circular rune-etched base plinth with floating soul wisps for glow, since that reads better as a hero prop than lying flat. I'm also confirming I need at least a root joint for the skeleton structure, possibly adding a few extra joints for hanging charms that could swing.

For the design itself, I'm sketching a roughly 2-meter tall dragonbone shaft rising from a 0.1m plinth, with a large curved blade at the top. I'm deciding the blade should extend along +X so its full silhouette reads clearly in the front view, rather than foreshortening it toward the camera like a creature's forward-facing +Z orientation.

For dragonbone styling, I'm envisioning stacked vertebrae segments like lathe bobbins in ivory bone with a subtly curving spine, topped by a dragon skull with horns at the shaft's peak — the blade itself emerging as a giant curved rib or wing-finger bone sweeping backward into a ghostly teal-green soul-fire glowing edge, following a Thresh/Soulstealer-style palette of bone ivory, deep teal-black metal, and high-contrast cyan-green glow accents.

I'm settling on spectral cyan-green #2ef2c0 as the dominant accent against dark charcoal-violet metal and ivory bone, with a small violet accent for contrast, giving a roughly 12-20 color flat palette plus paint variations. Now I'm laying out the structure in meters: a stepped hexagonal plinth from y=0 to 0.12 with a glowing rune-ring decal on top, and a spiked dark-metal ferrule with a teal glow gem socketing the scythe's butt into the plinth's center, possibly floating slightly above the base.

I'm planning the shaft from y=0.12 to 1.7 as a gentle S-curve with a thin radius, built around ~15 vertebra segments that mimic dragonbone, each with alternating spinous spikes and transverse fins, separated by small gaps that reveal a glowing teal sinew core running through the center. Below that I'm wrapping the lower grip section in dark leather with spiral gold/teal stripe paint, and mapping out the vertical zones: plinth, ferrule/butt with a downward spike and teal gem ring, then the lower shaft section beginning around 0.30.

Continuing the layout, I'm placing a bone claw ring around y~1.2 clutching a glowing soul orb as a mid-shaft hand-guard, with the vertebrae above growing larger and fanning into ribs toward 1.75, where a dragon skull crown sits at the top. I'm working out the skull's orientation relative to the blade -- deciding whether it faces forward toward +X with the blade extending from its back, or whether the blade should emerge differently so the composition reads correctly as a scythe head.

I'm settling on the skull in profile facing +X with its jaws clamping the root of the blade, which then sweeps outward as a large crescent curving downward at the tip, convex spine on top and concave cutting edge below, rooted near (0.05, 1.82) and curving toward a tip around (1.0, 1.45).

For the blade itself I'm designing a bone-tube spine with knuckle bumps and spikes, paired with a translucent teal glowing crescent body for a "soul blade" look, plus a darker bone-metal edge and rune paint decals to keep it readable at a glance.

Since paint can't actually glow, I'm layering an extruded dark-to-teal gradient blade body with a separate flat glowing teal edge sweep, then overlaying thin SVG-textured planes on both faces to carry the glowing runes, veins, and cracks matched to the blade's bounding box.

Now I'm working out the blade's geometric outline in meters—defining the spine curve and concave edge curve from root to tip using a centerline bezier with a tapering half-width function to shape the scythe's curved profile.

Still tuning the width functions...

I'll add ivory knuckle bumps at joints, sparse spike spurs along the dorsal spine, and three rib struts crossing from spine to edge like finger bones of a wing.

I'm placing thin bone rods from the spine out to the blade's edge at intervals, with translucent membrane stretched between them like a dragon wing, plus glowing rune patterns on the membrane panels. I'm working out the blade's orientation so the thickness extrudes correctly along the cross product of its outline axes, positioning it near the skull's jaw root and keeping the shaft centered on its axis.

I'm debating whether to give the shaft a subtle S-curve for dynamism or keep it straight with vertebrae placed along a path using tangent-aligned frames, leaning toward a minor curve in X since the blade's weight pulls that direction.

For the plinth, I'm thinking of adding floating soul wisps—small glowing ghost-skull shapes tethered by spirals hovering above it, plus a soul orb near the claw, while making sure the scythe's butt still touches the floor at y=0. I'm also considering a hanging charm off the skull's horn, maybe a chain with a tiny skull and teal flame.

Writing the plinth geometry...

Adding more glow ring geometry...

Then I'm placing four small bone/horn spikes at the plinth's cardinal corners, carved from dragonbone and ivory, pointing up and outward with a faint glow accent.

For the ferrule I'm shaping a dark lathed metal cone with ring details between y 0.14 and 0.36, wrapped by cardinal bone claw brackets that curve inward to grip the shaft. I'm deciding on the color palette here—leaning toward teal as the main accent, dark violet-black metal, and bone ivory, while skipping gold trim in favor of a deeper verdigris tone to keep the color blocking minimal and cohesive.

Now I'm working out the shaft's construction: a continuous glowing teal core running from y=0.30 to 1.85, visible through gaps between a stack of hourglass-shaped vertebra segments that encase it. I'm sketching the lathe profile for each vertebra and calculating spacing—about twelve vertebrae spanning 1.4 meters with roughly 0.112 pitch, considering whether they should taper or grow slightly thicker toward the base near the grip.

Now I'm planning the overall layout of the shaft: alternating segments of bone vertebrae and wrapped leather grips, since a scythe needs two hand-holds spaced apart. I'm settling on vertebrae from 0.34–0.60, a lower grip at 0.62–0.92, more vertebrae at 0.94–1.16, an upper grip at 1.18–1.44, another vertebra section at 1.46–1.72, then a collar and skull cap near the top—with the grips done in dark violet leather featuring teal stitch stripes and bone rings at their ends.

I'm thinking through how to build each vertebra procedurally, spacing them at roughly 0.11 intervals with spiky dorsal processes alternating front and back, plus small transverse winglets sticking out sideways. I want to add a rib cage feature partway up the shaft that curls outward to cradle a glowing soul orb, like a floating lantern cradled in bone—placing it around y 1.50–1.72 so the ribs bulge out to radius 0.11 and enclose an orb of radius 0.06–0.07 that partially conceals the shaft core at that point.

Now I'm working out the exact vertical layout from base to tip: plinth, ferrule with claws, pairs of vertebrae at specific y-intervals, lower and upper grip sections, then the rib cage with the soul orb around 1.53–1.75, followed by a skull collar and finally the dragon skull itself sitting atop the shaft facing forward with an open jaw, while making sure the blade's position in +X stays clear of the cage ribs' radius.

The dragon skull design has the blade root emerging from between the open jaws -- cranium as a scaled ellipsoid, snout as a tapering frustum extending forward, with upper and lower jaw pieces framing where the blade passes through and continues out to its tip.

Since the skull faces +X with camera at +Z, I confirm both eyes are visible from this profile angle. I'm positioning the blade root between the jaws at (0.05, 1.89), with the mouth gap defined by the upper jaw underside near y≈1.915 and lower jaw top near y≈1.86.

Reworking the blade geometry: making it emerge like a tongue from the mouth with a narrow root around x≈0.2, width ~0.06, then widening outward in a flame-like taper to about 0.14 before narrowing again toward the tip, using tapering functions for the top and bottom edge offsets along the spine curve.

Overall height comes to roughly 2.1m with horns included, and x-extent runs about -0.35 to 1.2, with the shaft centered at x=0. Now thinking about edge curvature—since the centerline curves downward toward the tip, the bottom edge is the inside of that curve, making it concave like a real scythe blade, so I need to work out the path normal to offset correctly.

I'm planning a layered construction: an ivory spine bone swept along the top line with tapering radius plus small knuckle-like bumps for a vertebra look, a glowing teal cutting edge swept along the bottom scalloped outline using a thin low-poly tube, and finger-like ribs connecting spine points to the scallop notch tips.

For the scallop shape itself, I'm working out a formula that modulates the base edge curve with an absolute-cosine term so it creates pointed fingertip peaks with smooth concave arcs between them, tuning the amplitude and frequency so the lobes land correctly between finger positions.

With sharp corners confirmed for m=4 peaks, I'm now placing finger bone rods running from the spine out to each peak point, tapering from 0.009 to 0.005 ivory radius. For the blade paint, I'm working out a gradient coloring scheme that blends dark violet near the spine into deep teal toward the edge, trying to figure out how to derive distance-from-spine using the point's relative position.

I'm computing the vertical offset from the spine curve by interpolating a sampled spine-y lookup against the x-coordinate, then normalizing that distance by blade width for the gradient factor. For the glowing rune details, I'm planning an SVG overlay mapped from meters to pixels, sized to cover the blade's bounding box, and considering whether each face of the blade plane needs its own mirrored texture since a plane only renders toward one side.

For the back-facing plane, I decide it's simpler to just rotate it 180° about the Y axis rather than flip the texture, accepting that the mirrored appearance is fine since the runes are invented glyphs anyway. For the glow rendering, I'm settling on opaque solid shapes with thick strokes for veins, rune glyphs inside membrane panels, and gradient-based color variation for the soft glow effect along edges, since alpha transparency gets clipped by the cutout logic.

Now I'm designing the panel coloring with a deep teal-violet gradient and glowing vein overlay. I'm also planning the floating soul elements: ghost-shaped card sprites with hollow eyes glowing cyan-green, arranged as 3-4 orbiting wisps at varied radii and heights, double-sided so they're visible from any angle, plus small sparkle spheres and a pair of thin spiraling soul-trail ribbons winding up around the central shaft.

For the hilt details, I'm adding a bone claw crossguard with four flaring spikes at the grip's top, and considering a hanging tassel or chain ornament — either a tiny skull charm dangling from the blade's spine or a ribbon tassel made of jointed box-section segments sweeping down from the grip ring in dark violet with teal tips.

For the rig, I'll keep it simple with a single root joint at the shaft base, letting the ribbon chain parent to it, and I'm planning a mottled bone material palette (base ivory, darker tones, and shadow tones) with grain texture to get that hand-painted LoL aesthetic within the triangle and material budget.

Now I'm settling on the metal and accent colors—dark purples for the base metal with teal highlights and a tiny hot purple accent, keeping the total palette within 64 colors.

For the grip, I'm designing a spiral paint function on a swept tube: diagonal bands alternate between dark leather texture and thin teal stitching, using a modulo pattern on the sweep coordinates to create the spiral stripe effect.

For the skull, I'm going with a mottled bone texture with a few glowing teal cracks, keeping the shading flat and painted like League of Legends style art.

Now I'm setting up the file imports and helper functions for building the 3D model, defining parts via direction and target point helpers before writing the vertex helper function.

Writing lathe geometry for vertebrae segments...

For the spinous processes, I'm placing small spikes alternating front and back along the Z axis at each vertebra, angling them outward from the spine to suggest a dragon's dorsal ridge.

I also want shorter transverse winglet spikes jutting out sideways from each vertebra, making the front-facing spikes slightly larger since they're more visible to the viewer. That gives roughly 32 spikes total across 8 vertebrae, which feels manageable, and now I'm double-checking the vertical spacing of each vertebra so the spikes don't collide with the upper grip region.

Let me stack the full height: lower vertebrae, lower grip, mid vertebrae, upper grip, then the cage with its orb, a collar ring, the skull base, and the head with horns, landing around 2.15m total. That's tall for a real scythe but fits a fantasy, LoL-style exaggerated weapon, and I'm checking that the grip heights still feel natural for hands holding the planted staff.

I'm working out the vertebra spacing so a thin glowing teal core shows through small gaps between segments — tightening the pitch to 0.115 with 0.1-tall vertebrae gives a believable 1.5cm gap of visible glow, and I'm recalculating the lower vertebrae positions with this new spacing.

Now I'm shaping the butt spike as a lathed metal cone profile that tapers and flares before narrowing into the plinth, then adding a glowing ring band partway down the spike using another small lathe shape.

I'm also planning small glowing octahedron gems embedded at the ferrule's ring positions, plus four curving claw-like talon shapes sweeping up from the plinth to grip the ferrule near the top.

For the plinth itself, I'm making it an 8-sided octagonal base with alternating bone spikes jutting outward and upward at the cardinal and corner points, creating a varied silhouette when viewed from above.

I'm also adding small teal glow gems embedded along the rim's step faces, plus a subtle glow ring along the top face path. For the soul vortex effect, I'm scripting two intertwined spirals that rise upward while shrinking in radius, using a helical path with defined turns, pitch, and tube thickness to create a glowing double-helix look.

Now I'm designing ghost-wisp soul cards as teardrop-shaped SVGs with a round head, wavy curling tail, and teal-white gradient fill, with dark circular eye cutouts, and placing five of them at scattered positions around the scene while keeping clear of the blade's bounding region, with each card framed to face upward.

Adding ember sparks and cage ribs...

Still refining the ring geometry with a closed catmull curve, then adding small lathed bone cups at top and bottom, plus a glowing orb sphere with layered shells for intensity.

Now I'm placing the upper grip and collar sections along the staff's height, then shifting to defining the skull: positioning a scaled sphere for the cranium and a tapered box frustum for the upper snout shape.

Now placing the nose knob and small dark nostril spheres near the tip, then adding brow ridge spikes angled back and up, plus dark eye socket recesses with small glowing teal eyeballs nested inside.

I'm adding a zygomatic arch rod for the cheekbone, then placing small ivory teeth spikes pointing downward along the snout's underside on both sides, and setting up a jaw hinge pivot for the lower jaw.

I'm angling the open lower jaw box downward with tapered dimensions, adding upward-pointing lower teeth and a chin spike, and defining a jaw joint so it can move—leaving a gap between the upper and lower jaw where a blade could emerge from the mouth.

I'm placing the blade root slightly inside the skull near x=0.06, then working out the horn geometry on each side — base near (−0.06,1.99) curving via bezier out to a tip around (−0.42,2.1).

Still refining horn curves... I'm thickening the horns with a tapering radius and adding darker growth-ring bands painted radially along their length, then adding a second smaller pair of cheek spikes lower on the skull.

I'm deciding against a central crest horn since it would crowd the silhouette, opting instead for just the paired main horns plus cheek spikes, and adding a small upward nose-tip spike near the snout for extra detail.

Now I'm working out bone knuckle spheres positioned along the spine curve, plus three dorsal back-spikes whose direction I derive from the curve's tangent rotated to point outward, before moving on to planning the glowing membrane overlay planes for the blade.

Still figuring out coordinate mapping...

Still writing SVG path logic...

I'm settling on a 960px texture size with thick bright teal glow strokes for the veins, and now planning deterministic rune glyphs (crosses, triangles, circles) placed at each panel's center between fingers.

Still writing glyph placement and rotation logic... I'm also mirroring the design onto the opposite face and figuring out blade body shading with a dark violet-to-teal gradient, adjusting the panel offsets to roughly 2.5mm from the blade surface for a cleaner extrusion.

Now I'm layering in teal flame-shaped cards rising from the blade's spine, around fourteen of them with varied sizes and glow intensity, giving it a wispy spectral effect, and considering adding similar drifting flame cards along the bottom edge as if souls are peeling off the blade.

I'm also thinking through the plinth top: a circular rune ring with concentric circles, twelve radial glyph ticks, and a cut-out center for the ferrule, rendered as a transparent-background SVG plane facing upward so the base shows through underneath.

Now I'm setting up the bone paint, layering a grain texture with a mottled pattern for a worn bone look.

For metal paint I'll countershade a dark purple base with a lighter top. Naming parts isn't necessary, and the plinth should sit flush at the base. I'll add gold accent rings at the grips and plinth using lathe segments, keeping total colors under 64 with my bone, metal, and glow variants. Then I'll build a spiral ribbon from the path spiral function and start a hanging tassel chain from the upper grip's top ring.

Now I'm working out the ribbon's path so it clears the spine's spikes — checking that the shaft and vertebra radii leave room, and realizing the front-facing spikes would collide with a ribbon hung straight down. I'm repositioning it diagonally between the spike axes so it clears their tips, calculating the offset distance needed at that 45-degree placement.

I'm also planning the ribbon geometry itself: a swept box cross-section tapering slightly, painted with a gradient from dark violet to teal with a gold hem, ending near a bone bead and glow gem, built from a chain of three or four catmull-spline joints.

For the skull, I'm setting up the bone hierarchy — a root/base joint at the origin, and a jaw joint attached to it so the jaw parts rotate around a hinge point while aiming toward the jaw tip. I need to be careful that skull parts without an explicit bone assignment don't accidentally snap to the jaw joint just because it's nearby, so I'm considering adding a dedicated "skull" joint near the base to serve as the default attachment point for those parts.

To avoid repeating bone assignments everywhere, I'm defining small helper functions that default options to a given bone — one for base, one for skull, one for jaw — so each shape call just spreads in its specific overrides. Defining color constants...

Defining more paint gradients...

Writing paint shader logic...

Still computing outline geometry...

I need the tip's top and bottom points to coincide exactly so I can drop the duplicate — setting the width function to zero at u=1 makes that work cleanly, and I'll just skip the bottom's final point to avoid a zero-length segment. Winding orientation shouldn't matter much for the extrude, so now I'm checking whether the bottom edge self-intersects anywhere.

Near the tip the centerline curves fairly sharply downward, turning clockwise, which means the inside of that turn is on the bottom (−n) side — so I need to check the radius of curvature there against the local width. Estimating from the tangent direction change, the curvature radius near the tip comes out to roughly 0.4, which should still be safely larger than the width at that point.

Now I'm defining the bone/spine path for the structure — placing it along the centerline offset slightly toward the top (n*0.6*a), sampled at a dozen points with a tapering radius function so the bone tube sits centered inside the membrane without poking through.

With world positioning anchored at a base offset, I'm building finger rods from the spine to peaks at three positions, each tapering, and adding small claw spikes at their tips. I'm also laying out a glow outline along the bottom edge using the existing bottom sample points as a thin teal polyline.

For the inner edge highlight, I'm sizing the tube slightly proud of the surface and splitting the polyline sweep at sharp corners while keeping it smooth elsewhere, using a reduced side count for efficiency. Now I'm setting up flame-textured card frames along the spine, oriented upward at each sample point with varied size and spacing.

Cards face front toward the viewer with the flow direction set so they read face-on with their crossed pairs, counting 12 total since the cross doubles them. For soul wisps hanging from the bottom edge, I'm flipping the flame orientation 180 degrees so they drip downward like inverted fire, giving them a smaller size than the spine flames.

Writing SVG code...

Still writing SVG code...

Skipping the skull emblems idea, I'm building the plinth with a lathe-based octagonal foundation, a rune disc on top, eight rim spikes alternating long and short lengths leaning outward, and glow gems placed on each of the eight faces to match the segment angles.

I'm not worrying about exact spike-to-face alignment since small mismatches won't matter visually, so I'll just use 8 segments and adjust the spin after previewing. I'm also adding a thin glowing ring at the base of the spikes, built from a closed 16-point circular path around the plinth.

For the claws gripping the shaft, I'm sketching four diagonal bezier curves curling inward from the plinth base toward tapered tips, each with a small knuckle sphere at the root for a gripping look.

Now I'm moving on to shading the skull parts — building the cranium as a flattened sphere with dark eye socket depressions and small glowing teal eye spheres positioned symmetrically, sized relative to the cranium's width at that point.

Adding brow spikes next, plus a trio of small nasal ridge spikes running along the top of the snout from back to front.

Now I'm reviewing the builder API shapes available to me—lathe, spike, rod, part, glow, and cards—to figure out which helpers fit best for the remaining geometry and texture work.

Checking frame and bone defaults next: an element with no explicit bone should fall back to the nearest joint, so I'll set the cards' bone to the base. For the horn surface I'm defining a paint function that bands colors along the sweep parameter, aiming for a gradient toward darker tips.

For the plinth rune ring I'm laying out concentric SVG circles at a 512 viewBox, sizing stroke widths and radii so the rune bands stay within the allowed plane thickness and clear the ferrule and claw elements without overlapping.

I'm adding twelve small glyph marks between radius 135 and 195, plus a six-point star made from two overlapping triangles for extra detail, then setting up a reusable glyph function that returns path shapes from a small template library for blade runes.

I'm converting the local blade coordinates into pixel space, mapping the x range to 960px and the y range to 480px, then checking the tip position and bottom scallop stay within the [-0.4, 0.2] vertical bounds.

I'm settling on a plane sized 1.2 by 0.62 units, scaled by 800 to get 960x496 pixels, centered at local point (0.6, -0.09), and setting up the blade texture plane facing +Z just offset from the center.

Now I'm checking orientation: the front plane facing +Z correctly maps u toward +X as viewed by someone looking down −Z, but the back plane facing −Z ends up mirrored — the viewer looking +Z sees their right as world −X, so the texture draws mirrored and needs to be flipped in X to match the blade shape correctly.

My fix is to generate a second texture by wrapping the same SVG content in a group transform that translates and scales by -1 in X, mirroring it for the back plane, which doubles the texture atlas size but stays well within limits. I note the rune plane on the plinth is fine as-is since its orientation doesn't have this issue, and I move on to practical build details: sweep radius as a function of t, passing path point arrays to sweep calls, bone attachment for sweeps, and random seeding for soul wisp and ember spark effects.

Before writing more code, I want to verify the actual API signatures -- how the rng function works, whether bezier accepts 3 or 4 control points, and what tangentAt and Path.at return -- so I need to check the source for frame imports and path methods.
